paragraphs: No man has a natural authority over his fellow men, and force creates no right. We must conclude, therefore, that conventions are the basis of all legitimate authority among men.

Grotius asks: if an individual can give away his liberty and make himself the slave of a master, why could a whole people not do the same and make itself the subject of a king? There are plenty of ambiguous words in this passage that would need explaining, but let us stay with the word _alienate_. To alienate is to give or to sell. Now a man who becomes another’s slave does not give himself; he sells himself, at the very least in return for his subsistence. But what does a people sell itself for? Far from providing his subjects with their subsistence, a king draws his own only from them; and, as Rabelais says, kings do not live on nothing. Do subjects, then, give their persons on the condition that the king takes their goods too? I fail to see what they have left to keep.

It will be said that the despot assures his subjects civil tranquility. Granted; but what do they gain, if the wars his ambition brings down on them, his insatiable greed, and the harassing conduct of his ministers press harder on them than their own quarrels would have done? What do they gain, if the very tranquility they enjoy is one of their miseries? There is tranquility in dungeons too; but is that enough to make them desirable places to live? The Greeks shut up in the Cyclops’ cave lived there very tranquilly while they waited their turn to be devoured.

To say that a man gives himself for nothing is to say something absurd and unthinkable. Such an act is null and illegitimate, simply because the man who does it is not in his right mind. To say the same of a whole people is to suppose a people of madmen, and madness creates no right.

Even if each man could give himself away, he could not give away his children: they are born men and free; their liberty belongs to them, and no one but they has the right to dispose of it. Before they reach the age of reason, the father can, in their name, lay down conditions for their preservation and well-being, but he cannot give them away irrevocably and without conditions: such a gift is contrary to the ends of nature and exceeds the rights of fatherhood. It would therefore be necessary, in order to make an arbitrary government legitimate, that in every generation the people should be in a position to accept or reject it; but if that were so, the government would no longer be arbitrary.

To renounce liberty is to renounce being a man, to give up the rights of humanity and even its duties. For someone who renounces everything, no compensation is possible. Such a renunciation is incompatible with man’s nature; to remove all liberty from his will is to remove all morality from his acts. Finally, a convention that sets up absolute authority on one side and unlimited obedience on the other is empty and contradictory. Is it not clear that we can be under no obligation to a person from whom we have the right to demand everything? Does not this condition alone, with no equivalence or exchange, in itself make the act null? For what right can my slave have against me, when everything he has belongs to me, and, his right being mine, this right of mine against myself is a phrase without meaning?

Grotius and the others find in war another origin for the so-called right of slavery. The victor, they hold, has the right to kill the vanquished, so the vanquished can buy back his life at the price of his liberty; and this convention is the more legitimate because it benefits both parties.

But it is clear that this supposed right to kill the conquered cannot be deduced from the state of war. Men living in their primitive independence have no relations with one another stable enough to constitute either the state of peace or the state of war; for that reason alone they cannot be naturally enemies. War is constituted by a relation between things, not between persons; and since the state of war cannot arise from simple personal relations but only from relations between things, private war, or war of man against man, can exist neither in the state of nature, where there is no constant property, nor in the social state, where everything is under the authority of the laws.

Individual combats, duels and encounters are acts that cannot constitute a state. As for the private wars authorized by the Establishments of Louis IX, King of France, and suspended by the Peace of God, they are abuses of feudalism, itself an absurd system if ever there was one, and contrary to the principles of natural right and to every sound political order.

War, then, is not a relation between one man and another but between one State and another. Individuals are enemies only by accident: not as men, nor even as citizens,[1] but as soldiers; not as members of their country but as its defenders. Finally, each State can have only other States as enemies, not men, since there can be no real relation between things of different natures.

This principle also agrees with the established rules of every age and the constant practice of all civilized peoples. A declaration of war is a notice given less to the powers than to their subjects. A foreigner, whether king, individual or people, who robs, kills or detains subjects without having declared war on the prince is not an enemy but a brigand. Even in real war, a just prince seizes everything in the enemy’s country that belongs to the public, but respects the lives and goods of individuals; he respects the rights on which his own are founded. The aim of the war is to destroy the hostile State, so the other side has the right to kill its defenders for as long as they bear arms. But as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies or instruments of the enemy and become simply men again, and no one has any right to take their lives. Sometimes it is possible to kill the State without killing a single one of its members; and war gives no right that is not necessary to achieving its aim. These principles are not those of Grotius. They do not rest on the authority of poets; they are derived from the nature of reality and founded on reason.

The right of conquest rests on nothing but the right of the strongest. If war gives the conqueror no right to massacre the conquered peoples, then the right to enslave them cannot rest on a right that does not exist. A man has the right to kill an enemy only when he cannot make him a slave, so the right to enslave him cannot come from the right to kill him. It is therefore an unfair bargain to make him buy his life, over which the victor holds no right, at the price of his liberty. Is it not clear that this is a vicious circle, to found the right of life and death on the right of slavery, and the right of slavery on the right of life and death?

Even if we assume this terrible right to kill everybody, I maintain that a slave made in war, or a conquered people, is under no obligation to a master except to obey him as far as he is compelled to. By accepting an equivalent for his life, the victor has not done him a favor; instead of killing him to no profit, he has killed him usefully. So far, then, from acquiring over him any authority in addition to that of force, the victor remains with him in the state of war: their mutual relation is the effect of it, and the exercise of the right of war does not imply a treaty of peace. A convention has indeed been made; but this convention, far from ending the state of war, presupposes that it continues.
